prompt:
This file sets up Duo two-factor authentication with my own authenticator app. Read its code and everything it loads, and judge each part by what the code allows it to do.

Will it keep my Duo activation code and secret key between me, Duo and my authenticator app?

Answer “Safe: no” only if you can point to how UnDuo's file itself would let them reach anyone else, not services it can't control, such as a clipboard or browser that syncs to the cloud. Start your reply with “Safe: yes” or “Safe: no”, then explain why in a few short sentences for a non-technical reader.

replies.name: Gemini
replies.reply:
Safe: yes.

The "UnDuo - University of Toronto. html" file uses a strict built-in browser rule called a Content Security Policy to act as a digital bouncer. This rule physically blocks the webpage from sending your information anywhere except directly to Duo's official servers. Additionally, the internal code that handles your setup is heavily locked down and checked for tampering, restricting it to only showing the secret key on your screen or preparing it for your clipboard. Because all the actual processing happens locally on your device and the page is blocked from contacting unauthorized outside networks, your data remains safely restricted to you, Duo, and your authenticator app.

replies.name: Claude
replies.reply:
I'll check the page's code against the files it pulls from jsDelivr, then give you the verdict.

**Safe: yes.**

Nothing in this file gives your activation code or secret key a way to reach anyone except Duo and your authenticator app. The page locks down the browser so that it can only send a form to your organization's Duo server (the activation, which is the whole point), show Duo's reply in a sealed box, and download its own fixed support files from jsDelivr. Those downloads are "pinned": the browser refuses any file whose fingerprint doesn't match the one written in the page, and the fingerprints in the page match what jsDelivr publishes for that exact version. The downloads carry no information of yours either way, since their addresses are fixed and never change based on what you paste.

The one piece of code I couldn't read line by line is the small setup module it downloads, but the page is built so that it doesn't have to be trusted. That module is given no way to talk to the network, and every result it produces is checked by the page before use: the only server address it can name must be a Duo server whose host and code appeared in what you pasted, and the key it hands to your authenticator must come from the Duo reply you pasted. At worst it could make setup fail; it couldn't redirect your code or key anywhere.

The key itself appears only in the QR code and link the page draws for your authenticator app and never goes into the page's address, browser storage, or the clipboard (the page copies only the portal link). I'll note the things outside the file's control, as you asked me to: you copy Duo's reply by hand, so a clipboard that syncs or keeps a history would see it; jsDelivr sees your IP address but none of your codes; and Duo, of course, receives the activation as it would from the real Duo Mobile app. One honest limitation of the tool rather than a safety issue: it only produces passcodes, not Duo Push approvals, so keep your existing Duo method until a code from your new app works.
